summary: An island nation in the Indian Ocean at the northern end of the Mozambique Channel off southeastern Africa, known for its spice production (vanilla and ylang-ylang), independent from France in 1975.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam was introduced between the 10th and 15th centuries by Arab, Persian (Shirazi) and Swahili merchants through Indian Ocean trade; in the Middle Ages the Comoros were part of the trade network of the Swahili coast, and from the 15th century several sultanates were established on the islands. Islam (the Sunni Shafi'i school) became the core of Comorian identity, and after independence in 1975 the constitution made Islam the state religion, so about 98% of the population are Muslim.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism arrived with French colonization, after France occupied Mayotte in 1841 and made the other three islands protectorates in 1886; its followers are mostly French and immigrants from Madagascar. Because Islam is deeply rooted in Comorian society, Catholics have always been a tiny minority, concentrated mainly in the capital Moroni.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: Other religions include Protestantism, Hinduism and traditional beliefs, with followers mostly foreign residents such as merchants from India and immigrants from Madagascar. Comorian law strictly restricts conversion to religions other than Islam, so the numbers of other religions are very small.

religion.background: The earliest inhabitants of the Comoros were probably Austronesian peoples from Southeast Asia and Bantu peoples of East Africa; later Arab, Persian and Swahili merchants brought Islam through Indian Ocean trade, and from the 15th century Islamic sultanates formed on the islands. From 1841 to 1912 France gradually colonized the four islands, and in 1975 the Comoros declared independence, but Mayotte chose to remain with France. After independence Islam became the state religion, and in 2018 a constitutional amendment made the Sunni Shafi'i school the national faith; Islamic culture deeply influences Comorian law, education and daily life.

language.official: The official languages are Comorian, French and Arabic.

ranking.name: Comorian
ranking.description: Comorian (Shikomori) belongs to the Bantu family and is close to Swahili, but is influenced by Arabic, French and Malagasy. Comorian has different dialects on the four islands, such as Shingazidja on Grande Comore and Shindzuani on Anjouan, and residents of the islands can broadly understand one another. Because it is the common mother tongue of Comorians, about 96% of the population use it as their main language, and since 2001 it has been an official language alongside French and Arabic.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French arrived with French colonization in the 19th century, was the language of administration and education in the colonial period, and remained an official language after independence in 1975. Because government, law, the media and higher education use French, most educated Comorians can use French, and in addition large numbers of Comorians have moved to places such as Marseille in France, which also keeps French in an important position in Comorian society.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic is the religious language of Islam, and Comorian children traditionally learn to read and write Arabic in Quranic schools; Comorian itself was formerly also written in the Arabic script. In 1993 the Comoros joined the Arab League and Arabic was made an official language, but very few have Arabic as their mother tongue, and it is used mainly for religion and in some educational settings.

language.history: Comorian originates from the Bantu languages of the East African coast and belongs to the same language group as Swahili; after the Middle Ages it absorbed a great deal of Arabic vocabulary and was long written in the Arabic script. After French colonization in the 19th century, French became the language of administration and education, and the Latin alphabet also gradually came to be used to write Comorian. After independence in 1975, Comorian, French and Arabic together made up the Comoros's linguistic landscape, and the 2001 constitution listed all three as official languages. In recent years the government has promoted standardizing Comorian in the Latin alphabet and strengthening mother-tongue education in schools.

ranking.name: Pilao (spiced pilaf)
ranking.description: Rice is simmered with meat (beef, chicken or mutton) and flavored with spices such as cloves, cinnamon and cardamom, a richly fragrant pilaf.
ranking.history: Pilao dates from the era of Indian Ocean trade, when Arab and Indian merchants carried the way of making pilaf (pilau) to the East African coast and the Comoros, and the name is the same as the East African Swahili 'pilau'. The Comoros are an important world producer of cloves and vanilla, and these spices give the local pilaf an especially rich flavor. It is an essential dish at weddings and festivals, especially in the traditional Comorian 'Grand Mariage', where it is indispensable.

ranking.name: Mataba (cassava leaves in coconut milk)
ranking.description: Cassava leaves are pounded and stewed with coconut milk, garlic and onion, sometimes with fish or meat added, with a creamy texture and coconut aroma, eaten with rice.
ranking.history: Mataba is the most representative home-cooked dish of the Comoros and is also popular in Mayotte, Madagascar and the East African coast. Cassava is native to South America and was brought to Africa by the Portuguese after the 16th century and then to the Indian Ocean islands; the coconut is the most common crop along the Comorian coast. This dish combines the two and is the most common dish on the everyday Comorian table.

ranking.name: Langouste à la vanille (vanilla lobster)
ranking.description: Lobster is cooked with Comorian vanilla pods, butter and cream, with a rich vanilla aroma, the most representative luxury dish of the Comoros.
ranking.history: The Comoros are one of the world's main vanilla-producing areas; in the 19th century French colonists introduced vanilla from Mexico and established vanilla plantations in the Comoros, Madagascar and Réunion. Vanilla requires hand pollination, and the growing and processing are very labor-intensive. Vanilla lobster combines the Comoros's rich seafood and vanilla, is regarded as a signature dish of the Comoros, and often appears in restaurants and on important occasions.

ranking.name: Coconut rice
ranking.description: Sweet, fragrant rice cooked with thick coconut milk and a little salt, with soft grains and a rich coconut aroma, often eaten with curry, stewed fish or bean dishes.
ranking.history: Coconut rice is a traditional dish along the Indian Ocean coasts, common from the East African Swahili coast to Madagascar and the Comoros. Rice was introduced to East Africa and Madagascar in the Middle Ages by Austronesian peoples and Indian Ocean trade, while coconuts are everywhere on tropical islands. In the Comoros, coconut rice is often prepared on Fridays (the Islamic day of congregational prayer) and at festivals, a common dish at family gatherings.

ranking.name: Sambusa (fried triangle pastries)
ranking.description: Thin pastry is filled with ground meat, onion and spices, folded into a triangle and deep-fried, with a crisp shell, often eaten to break the fast during Ramadan.
ranking.history: Sambusa shares its origin with India's 'samosa' and is generally thought to originate in Central Asia and the Middle East, reaching the East African coast through Indian Ocean trade with medieval merchants. In the Comoros and the Swahili region of East Africa, sambusa is an essential snack for breaking the fast at sunset during Ramadan. It also reflects the history of the Comoros as an Indian Ocean trading hub blending Arab, Indian and African food cultures.
